e-616.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions
e-616.problem:
The position vector $\mathbf{r}$ of a particle $P$ relative to a fixed origin $O$ at time $t > 0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 3t^3, 2t^2\rangle.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}.$
e-616.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨9{t}^{2},\,4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-617.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions at a Given Time
e-617.problem:
The position vector $\mathbf{r}$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t > 0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 12t, 2t^3\rangle.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}$ at time $t=1.$
e-617.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨12,6{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=1$, we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨12,6(1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨12,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

e-618.knowledge_point: Calculating the Speed of a Particle at a Given Time
e-618.problem:
The position vector $\mathbf{r}$ of a particle $P$ relative to a fixed origin $O$ at time $t > 0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 6t^2+2, 2t^3\rangle.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=2.$
e-618.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}+2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨12t,6{t}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=2$, we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨12(2),6(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨24,24⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=2$ we calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{v}(2),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(2)| & =\sqrt{{24}^{2}+{24}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2({24}^{2})} \\  & =24\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed when $t=2$ is $24\sqrt{2}\approx 33.94$ to two decimal places.

e-619.knowledge_point: Calculating the Times at Which a Particle Is Stationary
e-619.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle t^2-2t, t^3-3t \rangle, \quad t\in[0,\infty).
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
e-619.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,3{t}^{2}-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. This gives,

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2t-2,3{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}2t-2 & =0\,⇒\,t=1, \\ 3{t}^{2}-3 & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $t=-1$ is outside of the domain of $t,$ so we discard it. 

The solution $t=1$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only time when the object is stationary.

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨cos⁡(t2−1),4t−1⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v.

a
v=⟨2tsin⁡(t2−1),4⟩
b
v=⟨−sin⁡(t2−1),4⟩
c
v=⟨−sin⁡(t2−1),−4⟩
d
v=⟨−2tsin⁡(t2−1),4⟩
e
v=⟨−2tsin⁡(t2−1),−4⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Velocity is the derivative of position. By the chain rule, d/dt cos(t²−1) = −2t sin(t²−1), and d/dt(4t−1) = 4. Therefore option d is correct.

$$

$$

$$

The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+3}},2+2(3)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{2},\,2+6⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,8⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
r=⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t>0.

after.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨−cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v at time t=π2.

a
v(π2)=⟨1,0⟩
b
v(π2)=⟨−1,0⟩
c
v(π2)=⟨1,−1⟩
d
v(π2)=⟨−1,1⟩
e
v(π2)=⟨0,1⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector: v=drdt=⟨dxdt,dydt⟩=⟨ddt(−cos⁡t),ddt(sin⁡t)⟩=⟨sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩

To find the velocity when t=π2, we substitute into the above: v(π2)=⟨sin⁡(π2),cos⁡(π2)⟩=⟨1,0⟩

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms v(t)=⟨sin(t),cos(t)⟩, so v(π/2)=⟨1,0⟩. Option a is correct; the deliberately incorrect submission selected b.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions at a Given Time
content.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10

The position vector r of a particle P (relative to a fixed origin O) at time t is given by r=⟨t+4,ln⁡(5t+1)⟩,t>0. Calculate the velocity vector v at time t=3.

a
v(3)=⟨1,4ln⁡2⟩
b
v(3)=⟨1,54⟩
c
v(3)=⟨7,516⟩
d
v(3)=⟨7,4ln⁡2⟩
e
v(3)=⟨1,516⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Differentiating gives v(t)=⟨1,5/(5t+1)⟩. At t=3, v(3)=⟨1,5/16⟩, so option e is correct.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨t+4,\operatorname{ln}⁡(5t+1)⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=3.$
after.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+4),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5t+1))⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\frac{5}{5t+1}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=3,$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨1,\frac{5}{5(3)+1}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\frac{5}{16}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨t+4,\operatorname{ln}⁡(5t+1)⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=3.$
content.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+4),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5t+1))⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\frac{5}{5t+1}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=3,$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨1,\frac{5}{5(3)+1}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\frac{5}{16}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Question 17
?

A particle P moves in the x-y plane (relative to a fixed origin O) with position vector r=⟨t3−3t,2t2+6t−3⟩,t>0. Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.

a
The particle is never stationary
b
t=4
c
t=2
d
t=3
e
t=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the velocity vector v. Differentiating the position vector, we get v=drdt=⟨dxdt,dydt⟩=⟨ddt(t3−3t),ddt(2t2+6t−3)⟩=⟨3t2−3,4t+6⟩=⟨3(t2−1),2(2t+3)⟩=⟨3(t−1)(t+1),2(2t+3)⟩

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero: v(t)=0⟨3(t−1)(t+1),2(2t+3)⟩=⟨0,0⟩

So we need 3(t−1)(t+1)=0⇒t=±1,2(2t+3)=0⇒t=−32.

There is no value of t that satisfies both equations, so there are no stationary points.

content.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
r=⟨{t}^{3}-3t,\,2{t}^{2}+6t-3⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-3t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+6t-3)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-3,4t+6⟩ \\  & =⟨3({t}^{2}-1),2(2t+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨3(t-1)(t+1),2(2t+3)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨3(t-1)(t+1),2(2t+3)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3(t-1)(t+1)=0\, & ⇒\,t=\pm 1, \\ 2(2t+3)=0\, & ⇒\,t=-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

There is no value of $t$ that satisfies both equations, so there are no stationary points.
